title: Genetic and Clinical Determinants of Variation in Drug Response in Type 2 Diabetes: Insights From the Scottish and UK Biobank Cohorts
chunk_excerpt:
Our combined analyses show that both routinely measured clinical characteristics and inherited genetic variation contribute to heterogeneity in glycaemic response to glucose‐lowering therapies in type 2 diabetes, although their relative impact differs substantially.

Clinical variables emerged as the dominant determinants of treatment response across all drug classes. In particular, baseline HbA1c consistently explained the largest proportion of variability in glycaemic outcomes, with additional contributions from age and lipid measures that were broadly consistent across therapies. In contrast, factors such as BMI, renal function, sex and diabetes duration showed drug‐specific associations, likely reflecting differences in mechanisms of action between therapies. The consistency of these findings across independent cohorts supports their robustness and reinforces the central role of routinely collected clinical data in guiding treatment decisions.

In parallel, our genetic analyses show that polygenic risk contributes to treatment response in a drug‐class‐specific and biologically meaningful manner. At a global level, higher genetic liability to type 2 diabetes was associated with improved response to sulfonylureas, replicating previous findings reported by Li et al. [27] and supporting the hypothesis that individuals with greater β‐cell dysfunction benefit more from insulin secretagogues [28].

title: Concurrent Diabetic Muscle Infarction and JAK2 Exon 12-Positive Polycythemia Vera: A Rare Dual Diagnosis
chunk_excerpt:
Diabetic muscle infarction should be considered in patients with longstanding, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presenting with acute or subacute atraumatic limb pain and swelling. Early recognition of its characteristic MRI findings allows prompt diagnosis, avoids unnecessary muscle biopsy, and facilitates appropriate conservative management. This case illustrates the importance of investigating persistent erythrocytosis and thrombocytosis rather than attributing these abnormalities solely to the inflammatory response. Comprehensive hematological evaluation led to the diagnosis of JAK2 exon 12-positive polycythemia vera, a distinct condition requiring disease-specific management. Although the coexistence of diabetic muscle infarction and polycythemia vera is exceptionally uncommon, this case emphasizes the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis and avoiding premature diagnostic closure. Careful integration of clinical assessment, imaging findings, laboratory investigations, and multidisciplinary collaboration enabled accurate diagnosis and timely treatment of two independent disorders.

Additional case reports and larger observational studies are needed to better define the clinical significance of this uncommon association and determine whether it has implications for diagnosis, management, or prognosis.

title: HDAC3-driven immunometabolic reprogramming in type 2 diabetes and its complications: from enzymatic deacetylation to non-enzymatic scaffolding
chunk_excerpt: Accumulating clinical evidence supports the involvement of HDAC3 in the pathogenesis of T2DM. A community-based case-control study in China identified three single-nucleotide polymorphisms in HDAC3, namely rs11741808, rs2547547, and rs2530223, that are associated with an increased risk of T2DM (92). Consistent with this genetic association, both the expression and enzymatic activity of HDAC3 are markedly elevated in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from individuals with T2DM and correlate positively with inflammatory status, poor glycemic control, and impaired insulin sensitivity (9). Interestingly, adipose tissue from individuals with obesity exhibits reduced HDAC3 levels compared with that of normal-weight women, and HDAC3 mRNA expression and activity are negatively associated with inflammatory markers, obesity indices, and insulin levels, suggesting a complex and context-dependent role in metabolic dysregulation (76). Functionally, elevated HDAC3 not only impairs pancreatic β-cell function and promotes β-cell apoptosis (75), but also disrupts insulin signaling (72). Mechanistically, HDAC3 deacetylates insulin receptor substrate-2 (IRS2) and suppresses its transcription, thereby inhibiting the PI3K-AKT pathway and reinforcing a vicious cycle of inflammation and IR (93, 94).

title: Bile acid signaling in health and disease
chunk_excerpt: Preclinically, CYP8B1 deficiency or knockdown improves metabolic parameters by reducing CA-dependent lipid emulsification, promoting distal fatty acid absorption, and stimulating L-cell GLP-1 secretion, thereby enhancing glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity [308]. Concurrently, BA composition shifts toward hydrophilicity, increasing fecal lipid and BA excretion, preventing cholesterol-driven NAFLD, and blocking hypercholesterolemia in models of hepatic insulin signaling defects and type 1 diabetes [309]. In humans, CYP8B1 loss-of-function carriers show reduced 12α-hydroxylated BA proportions [310] and require higher glucose infusion rates during hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps, confirming enhanced peripheral insulin sensitivity [307]. Mechanistically, the altered CDCA/CA ratio strengthens insulin signaling and glucose uptake via the CDCA–FOXO1 axis. Given CYP8B1 is non-essential for viability, its inhibition offers a safe therapeutic strategy. Small-molecule inhibitors (e.g., MO-10 analogs) and indirect modulators (e.g., thyroid hormone analogs) are currently under development, representing promising approaches to remodel BA signaling for metabolic disease treatment.

title: Study variation in estimating Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) from serum creatinine, cystatin C, age, and sex
chunk_excerpt: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is widely considered the best indicator of kidney function but it cannot be measured directly. Instead, standard clinical practice is to calculate an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) using estimating equations based on serum concentrations of endogenous filtration markers, usually creatinine and/or cystatin C, and demographic variables such as age and sex. Current guidelines recommend creatinine-based eGFR (eGFRcr) for general use, with cystatin C–based eGFR (eGFRcys) or combined eGFRcr-cys used when greater accuracy is needed [1]. The Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equations for estimating GFR [2] are the most common equations used for adults in practice [1,3].

title: Biomarkers and Risk Prediction in Cardiovascular–Kidney–Metabolic Syndrome: A Comprehensive Review
chunk_excerpt: Kidney function biomarkers include estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and albuminuria [9]. These biomarkers are essential for identifying and monitoring kidney dysfunction in CKM syndrome. eGFR is calculated by serum creatinine or cystatin C, or by renogram. Serum creatinine remains the cornerstone of kidney function assessment, while cystatin C provides an alternative marker that is less influenced by muscle mass and diet [9]. The development of new creatinine- and cystatin C-based equations to estimate GFR without race has improved the accuracy of kidney function assessment and addressed important concerns about racial bias in clinical algorithms [9]. Renogram can detect the function of each kidney. Albuminuria and urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) serve as a sensitive marker of kidney damage and cardiovascular risk [10]. Claudel and Verma [10] provided a comprehensive state-of-the-art review of albuminuria in cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic disorders, highlighting its role as a key biomarker that reflects both kidney damage and systemic vascular dysfunction. These biomarkers may not adequately reflect the early stages of kidney injury or the complex interactions between kidney function and other organ systems. There are also studies of kidney tubular biomarkers over the past decades, such as urinary kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) and neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), which can indicate the early kidney injury [11,12]. However, these novel biomarkers have not been applied in clinical practice.

A decline in renal function was defined as any transition to a higher KDIGO stage, including substage progression within stage 3 (e.g., from G3a to G3b). Patients classified as G5 at baseline were therefore excluded from the analysis regarding KDIGO stage progression because further deterioration could not be captured within the KDIGO classification.

Recommended additional assessment based on albuminuria was not performed due to the lack of routine measurements during the included patients' hospital stays.

chunk_excerpt: As with all prediction equations, regression models for GFR estimates describe the average relationship between markers and mGFR with reasonable precision, but the uncertainty becomes much larger when applied to an individual. Our results provide quantification of the uncertainty in the eGFR. The magnitude of the uncertainty is consequential when eGFR values are close to decision thresholds. Small differences in eGFR may influence CKD staging, referral to nephrology, eligibility for therapies, medication dosing, or decisions to obtain confirmatory testing. In practice, this means that consistent with current clinical practice guidelines, an eGFR near a classification or referral threshold should be interpreted in clinical context, and confirmatory testing with cystatin C, combined creatinine-cystatin C eGFR, or measured GFR may be appropriate when the result would change management{, 2024 #185}. We were not able to incorporate all information that might be available to clinicians, such as extremes of muscle mass or diet. Prior work has not found that including common diseases or treatments as variables has improved the performance of creatinine-based eGFR equations [12]. Although “disease-specific” or “treatment-specific” eGFR equations could reduce variability in select populations, they may be impractical in clinical practice, as patients generally have more than one disease and undergo more than one treatment [13,14].

chunk_excerpt: eGFR based on serum creatinine is widely used in clinical practice to evaluate KF. In the present study, the CKD‐EPI equation was applied to estimate eGFR, as this formula is recommended by the KDIGO 2024 guidelines for being more applicable in the elderly [23]. Evidence indicates that it serves as a good general screening tool for KF, with the advantage of incorporating age and sex into the estimating equation. Additionally, this formula accounts for the complex physiological changes of the kidney and provides a more accurate assessment of renal function in older adults, thereby facilitating disease staging and stratified management [23]. As an effective screening instrument for KF, eGFR benefits from the inclusion of age, race, and sex in its calculation. Although ACR is not yet widely adopted, current European and North American guidelines recommend its use for assessing end‐organ damage in individuals with diabetes, hypertension, and CKD. A meta‐analysis indicated that albuminuria is associated with up to a 35% increased risk of CI [27]. Previous research has demonstrated that albuminuria reflects widespread microvascular endothelial injury in the kidney and an elevated cerebral vascular burden [28]. Endothelial cells are tightly interconnected to prevent hydrophilic substances from entering the brain. Endothelial damage can disrupt the BBB, leading to increased β‐amyloid levels and hyperphosphorylated tau, thereby exacerbating CI and dementia [29]. Furthermore, increased cerebral vascular load may also contribute to CI by aggravating neuroinflammation [28].

chunk_excerpt:
Overall, SGLT-2 inhibitors demonstrated a favorable safety profile across randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and real-world observational studies. The incidence of serious adverse events was generally comparable to placebo or standard therapy, supporting the use of SGLT-2 inhibitors in patients with chronic kidney disease, including those without diabetes [6,7,12,13,25,27].

Meta-analytic evidence demonstrated that SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of acute kidney injury among patients with CKD (RR 0.82; 95% CI, 0.72-0.93) [27]. This protective effect is consistent with broader trial-level evidence demonstrating favorable kidney outcomes in patients both with and without diabetes [25]. Although volume depletion is a recognized adverse effect of SGLT-2 inhibition, appropriate clinical monitoring is warranted, particularly in patients at increased risk of hypovolemia.

title: Recurrent Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis Weeks After SGLT2 Inhibitor Cessation: A Case Report
chunk_excerpt:
Sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are considered second‐line treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, with additional indications for heart failure and chronic kidney disease due to their cardiorenal protective effects [1, 2]. Although these medications are widely used and their efficiency has been documented and supported by the literature, they carry a small but important risk of EDKA, characterized by ketonemia, metabolic acidosis, and a high anion gap despite normal to mildly elevated plasma glucose levels [3]. The overall prevalence of EDKA in patients on SGLT2 inhibitor drugs is relatively low [4]. However, the number of cases presenting as EDKA is increasing, probably due to the increased use of this drug class in the treatment of diabetes [3–5].

EDKA is often challenging to diagnose, especially in the intensive care unit (ICU), where high anion gap metabolic acidosis is frequently attributed to acute kidney injury or lactic acidosis secondary to septic shock and other causes of tissue hypoperfusion [6]. Sepsis, surgery, reduced oral intake, and reduced insulin doses are known risk factors for SGLT2‐associated EDKA [7, 8]. Perioperative and postprocedural cases demonstrate that EDKA can occur despite the discontinuation of SGLT2 inhibitors many days before the triggering event and that prolonged glucosuria and ketonuria might be observed [9, 10].

title: Hospitalisation Is a Strong Risk Factor for Discontinuation of Sodium‐Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors for Type 2 Diabetes
chunk_excerpt:
Sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are a pillar of therapy for people with type 2 diabetes, heart failure (HF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) [1]. The continuation of these medicines for people who can tolerate them is critical. Even 30 days without continued empagliflozin use in people with HF is associated with a significant increased risk of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation [2].

SGLT2i are often paused in hospital in part because of the rare risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), with the aim to re‐start therapy once discharged (provided no contraindications) [3]. However, recent evidence suggests that therapy may not be restarted after hospital discharge, with close to 30% of SGLT2i‐treated people with type 2 diabetes hospitalised for HF discontinuing therapy in the 90 days following discharge [4]. Most of these people did not re‐initiate therapy within the year post‐hospitalisation. This is highly concerning as people with HF are at very high risk of adverse outcomes and hospitalisation should be a catalyst for initiation, not discontinuation, of these medicines. A Danish study similarly found one‐third of people initiating SGLT2i who discontinued therapy had a hospitalisation in the 3 months prior to discontinuation, although they did not explicitly test for associations between hospitalisation and discontinuation [5]. These findings raise questions as to whether hospitalisation is disruptive to the use of SGLT2i.

The renoprotective effects observed in individual randomized controlled trials have been further supported by multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Collectively, the included meta-analyses demonstrated that SGLT-2 inhibitors reduce the risk of CKD progression and adverse kidney outcomes while preserving kidney function across diverse patient populations [12,13,23-28]. Importantly, these benefits were observed across a broad range of baseline kidney function and were maintained in individuals with and without diabetes [25].

Meta-analytic evidence further demonstrated that SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy significantly slowed the annual decline in eGFR, supporting preservation of kidney function compared with control therapy [26,27]. Importantly, subgroup analyses showed that the renal benefits were consistent irrespective of baseline diabetes status, with a similar reduction in kidney disease progression observed in patients without diabetes (RR 0.69; 95% CI, 0.57-0.82), supporting the concept that the nephroprotective effects of SGLT-2 inhibitors extend beyond glucose lowering [25].

title: Autophagy and Mitophagy in Hypertensive Chronic Kidney Disease: Evidence Grading, Cell-Type Divergence, and a Working Lysosomal Hypothesis
chunk_excerpt:
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce kidney disease progression across diabetic and nondiabetic CKD and are standard therapy in much of the population relevant to this review. Experimental studies, predominantly in diabetic renal models, have linked their effects to activation of AMPK and SIRT1, suppression of mTORC1 and maladaptive HIF-1α signaling, and improvement in autophagy-associated and mitochondrial phenotypes [144,145,146,147]. These observations provide biological plausibility but do not establish autophagy as the mechanism underlying clinical renoprotection.

Viewed through the ACGEM framework, much of this evidence relies on upstream signaling or static autophagy-associated measurements rather than cell-type-resolved in vivo flux. In addition, SGLT2 inhibitors have major nonautophagic actions, including restoration of tubuloglomerular feedback, reduction of proximal tubular workload, and hemodynamic effects. Thus, direct evidence that modulation of autophagic flux mediates their benefit specifically in hypertensive kidneys remains lacking.

Sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT‐2) inhibitors inhibit the reabsorption of glucose from the urine in the proximal renal tubule and thereby lower blood sugar levels by increasing its excretion [1]. Due to their effectiveness, they have become a key drug class in the treatment of Type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, treatment with SGLT‐2 inhibitors, such as empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, showed clinical benefits on cardiovascular outcomes [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and mortality [7, 8] not only in T2D patients, but also in non‐diabetic patients. For this reason, potential mechanisms beyond glucose control mediating clinical SGLT‐2 effects have come into focus [9, 10].

One potential mechanism could be that SGLT‐2 inhibitors reduce endogenous and potentially harmful substances produced by the gut microbiome. According to a study by Billing et al., the concentration of uremic toxins decreased under therapy with SGLT‐2 inhibitors in mice and in addition, there was a broad downregulation of transport proteins in the kidney [11]. With this in mind, the cardiovascular and renal risk marker trimethylamine‐N‐oxide (TMAO) becomes a subject of interest.

title: The Role of Autoimmune Diseases in the Development of Aortic Aneurysms
chunk_excerpt:
Chronic inflammation is a hallmark of autoimmune diseases and serves as a critical mechanism in the pathogenesis of AAs. Persistent immune activation leads to the recruitment of inflammatory cells such as macrophages, lymphocytes, and neutrophils to the vascular wall. These infiltrating immune cells release pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α], interleukin-6 [IL-6]), chemokines, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) that exacerbate endothelial dysfunction and damage vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). Over time, this inflammatory milieu weakens the structural integrity of the aortic wall.

The role of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, TNF-α) and chemokines (IL-8, CCL1, CCL5) as crucial regulators of inflammation in the development of AAs was initially suggested by studies of individual cytokine proteins, and later confirmed using protein multiplex assays [24,25,26,27]. The same cytokines/chemokines have also been implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of autoimmune diseases, particularly SLE and RA [28,29,30,31,32,33]. Recent studies employing methodologies such as single-cell sequencing and Mendelian randomization have revealed additional candidate proteins relevant for AAs, such as the chemokine CXCL10 and the fibroblast growth factor FGF5 [34]. Importantly, CXCL10 has also been implicated in autoimmune diseases, namely SLE [35].

chunk_excerpt: Kidney function biomarkers include estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and albuminuria [9]. These biomarkers are essential for identifying and monitoring kidney dysfunction in CKM syndrome. eGFR is calculated by serum creatinine or cystatin C, or by renogram. Serum creatinine remains the cornerstone of kidney function assessment, while cystatin C provides an alternative marker that is less influenced by muscle mass and diet [9]. The development of new creatinine- and cystatin C-based equations to estimate GFR without race has improved the accuracy of kidney function assessment and addressed important concerns about racial bias in clinical algorithms [9]. Renogram can detect the function of each kidney. Albuminuria and urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) serve as a sensitive marker of kidney damage and cardiovascular risk [10]. Claudel and Verma [10] provided a comprehensive state-of-the-art review of albuminuria in cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic disorders, highlighting its role as a key biomarker that reflects both kidney damage and systemic vascular dysfunction. These biomarkers may not adequately reflect the early stages of kidney injury or the complex interactions between kidney function and other organ systems. There are also studies of kidney tubular biomarkers over the past decades, such as urinary kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) and neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), which can indicate the early kidney injury [11,12]. However, these novel biomarkers have not been applied in clinical practice.

chunk_excerpt: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is widely considered the best indicator of kidney function but it cannot be measured directly. Instead, standard clinical practice is to calculate an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) using estimating equations based on serum concentrations of endogenous filtration markers, usually creatinine and/or cystatin C, and demographic variables such as age and sex. Current guidelines recommend creatinine-based eGFR (eGFRcr) for general use, with cystatin C–based eGFR (eGFRcys) or combined eGFRcr-cys used when greater accuracy is needed [1]. The Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equations for estimating GFR [2] are the most common equations used for adults in practice [1,3].

chunk_excerpt: The clinical benefits observed are accompanied by an early functional reduction in glomerular filtration followed by slower long-term loss of kidney function. Initiation of SGLT2 inhibition is commonly followed by an early functional “dip” in eGFR. This decline is generally interpreted as a consequence of reduced intraglomerular pressure rather than structural injury [2, 10]. Trajectory analyses showed that, after the initial decline, eGFR decreased more slowly with dapagliflozin than with placebo, supporting longer-term preservation of kidney function [142]. Early reductions in urinary albumin excretion are also associated with subsequent kidney outcomes and may provide a clinically useful marker of treatment response [143]. Nevertheless, clinicians may remain hesitant to initiate treatment in advanced kidney disease or in older and clinically vulnerable populations. Analyses of patients with stage 4 CKD (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) reported sustained effects on eGFR decline without evidence of a disproportionate increase in safety concerns [144]. Evidence in older patients with CKD similarly supports careful individualised use rather than exclusion based solely on age [145]. These randomised trial findings are consistent with large real-world datasets. The Japan CKD Database reported lower renal event rates and slower kidney function decline among patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors than among those receiving other glucose-lowering therapies in routine clinical practice [146].
